findings.breaking_input: A rendered command whose source front matter has `allowed-tools` but whose rendered `.opencode/commands/<cmd>.md` file is missing or whose front matter `agent:` line is absent
findings.why: `commandFence` returns null when the command file is missing or has no `agent:` line, so the session runs with no fence even though the source grants tools via `allowed-tools`. The NO-FENCE refusal only fires when the file exists and names a fence that's missing. A stale or deleted render silently degrades to unfenced, undoing ADR-2027's whole point.
findings.fix: Treat a command with `allowed-tools` in its source (or a missing command file where one is expected) as an error: refuse NO-FENCE rather than returning null. Only a command whose source genuinely has no `allowed-tools` may run unfenced.

findings.breaking_input: A malicious `.opencode/commands/evil.md` in the cwd that contains `agent: legit-fence` where `legit-fence` exists but was rendered for a different command, e.g. `agent: arc-commit-fence` while the command file is `evil.md`
findings.why: `commandFence` only checks that the named agent is `-fence` and that `agents/<agent>.md` exists. It never verifies that the agent file actually corresponds to this command's fence. So an attacker-controlled command file can name any existing fence agent (e.g. arc-commit-fence) and run the session with a fence meant for a different, more privileged command. That fence may allow tools like `gh`, `vercel`, `git` the evil command should not have.
findings.fix: Bind the fence to the command: require `agent == <command>-fence` exactly (already done) AND verify the rendered fence file was produced by this command's own render (e.g. check the fence's allowed-tools match the command's source, or store a per-command fence name in a manifest). Simplest: refuse unless `agent === command + \"-fence\"` and the fence file's `description` or a marker names the command.

findings.breaking_input: A file under `.ops/` or any root outside `.codex/`, `.opencode/`, `.agents/skills/` rendered by a target
findings.why: `selfPlanFrom` checks `path.startsWith(r)` for the three roots, but `path` is arbitrary from the render. A render that produces `../outside` or a path with a leading `../` or an absolute path like `/etc/passwd` — or `AGENTS.md` itself — passes the startsWith check if it begins with one of the roots only when it's under them. But a render could produce `../../x` which startsWith `.codex/` false. Actually the vulnerable case: a render yields `.codex/../AGENTS.md`, which `startsWith(".codex/")` is true, and then the writer does `join(tree, path)` normalizing to `AGENTS.md` and `writeFileSync` overwrites the brain. The check is lexical, not canonicalized.
findings.fix: Canonicalize `path` (resolve and verify it stays inside `tree` plus one of the three roots) before accepting it; reject any `..` segment or absolute path. Apply the same confinement used for ADR-2024 manifest paths.

findings.breaking_input: A symlink at `.opencode/commands` pointing to `/somewhere/else` with files the render also produces; or a symlinked file under `.opencode/`
findings.why: `onDisk` uses `lstatSync` and treats a symlink as an extra file itself, not following it. That's safe for discovery. But when writing, `writeFileSync` follows symlinks. If a prior install (or an attacker) placed `.opencode/commands` as a symlink to an external directory, `mkdirSync(dirname(abs))` is a no-op and `writeFileSync(abs, text)` writes through the symlink into the target dir, escaping the tree. `--check` would flag the symlink as extra, but only when run; the writer runs without check in normal `--self`.
findings.fix: In the writer, refuse to write through a symlink: `lstatSync` any existing path component and error (`Refused(\"symlink\", ...)`) rather than following it, or unlink a symlink and write a real file.

findings.breaking_input: On POSIX, `finalise` with a live leader calls `treePids(child.pid)` which returns `[root]` only, then `killTree` kills the process group. If the leader reaped its group but a grandchild detached into a new session (setsid), the group kill misses it. The `.pid` file records only on Windows.
findings.why: `treePids` on POSIX returns `[root]` regardless of the actual tree, and the `seen`/record logic is Windows-only. So a detached grandchild that created its own process group survives `killTree`, and `survivors([root], true)` only checks the leader's group, never the detached process. The run exits 0/ok, leaving an orphan that can keep spending. This is exactly debt row 23's shape, but the fix only covers Windows.
findings.fix: On POSIX, discover the process tree via `ps --ppid` walk before killing, and poll survivors of each encountered pid, not just the leader's group. Record the tree in the `.pid` file on POSIX too.

findings.breaking_input: `finalise` reads `child.exitCode`/`signalCode` and if null assumes the leader is alive. But if the leader is a zombie that exited and was reaped synchronously (not via handler), `exitCode` may be set to null while the process is gone and the group reaped. `leading` becomes true and `treePids` walks a dead leader. Minor. The real issue: `survivors` polls `process.kill(pid, 0)` which on a zombie returns true forever (zombies are alive until reaped by init), so `left` stays non-empty and the run exits 7 KILL-INCOMPLETE even though the tree is actually gone.
findings.why: `alive` returns true for a zombie pid (ESRCH only when fully reaped; a zombie gives EPERM? No — a zombie is a valid pid, kill 0 succeeds). After `killTree` sends SIGKILL to the group, the leader becomes a zombie that the wrapper never `waitpid`s (it was uses `spawn` and may have already read the exit, but a zombie stays). `survivors` sees it alive for the full 5s and reports a survivor, misclassifying a clean kill as KILL-INCOMPLETE, and the `.pid` file is never unlinked, so the next run tries to reap a dead process.
findings.fix: Distinguish zombie from live: on POSIX read `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 3 for 'Z', or use `ps -o stat=` and treat 'Z' as not alive. Also `waitpid` the child to reap it before polling.

findings.breaking_input: `reapStale` on Windows deletes the `.pid` file with `unlinkSync` after killing, but if `killTree` inside the loop sets a verdict? No. The real gap: `reapStale` calls `killTree({pid})` for each live pid, but `killTree` may spawn `taskkill` and if it fails silently the pid is still alive; then `survivors` polls and if a survivor remains it `throw Refusal(\"STALE-RUN\")`. That refusal happens before the pidfile is unlinked, leaving it for next time. OK. The gap: `commandLine(pid) === t.cmd` comparison is exact string equality; Windows' CommandLine may have canonicalized quotes or casing so an equal-looking command differs, making a live OpenCode appear not-live and the pidfile cleared while the process keeps spending.
findings.why: The pid-reuse guard compares the stored command line to the current one with `===`. Windows PowerShell's `CommandLine` output can differ in quoting or case from what was stored (the stored string came from the same source, so usually identical, but a process can change its own command line via `SetCommandLine` or a sanitize). If it differs, the live process is not killed, the pidfile is `unlinkSync`'d, and the run proceeds with an orphan that can keep spending. The whole point of the check is defeated by any command-line mutation.
findings.fix: Treat "cannot confirm identity" as refuse-to-clear: if the pid is alive but its command line differs, refuse STALE-RUN instead of clearing. Never clear a pidfile naming a live pid.

findings.breaking_input: A repository where a generated directory like `.codex/` contains a tracked file that is also modified in the diff range (a hand-edit that CI's `--check` would catch). The exclusions skip it silently.
findings.why: `GENERATED` paths are excluded by exact prefix matches. If a source edit lands in the same commit as a stale generated file, the generated file is excluded from the diff shown to the attacker, but the commit-time check (`arc compile --self --check`) would fail. The attacker cannot see the stale-rerender evidence, but that's the design (regenerated and checked). The real issue: a file that is *both* source and generated (e.g. a new file under `.opencode/` that the render also produces) is always hidden, so a hand-planted malicious `.opencode/command/evil.md` that is also a rendered output would be invisible in the diff.
findings.fix: Only exclude files whose content equals a fresh render; if a generated-path file's diff is not byte-identical to a render of that path, include it in the diff. That keeps hand-planted or stale files visible.

findings.breaking_input: `arc compile --self --check` with an extra argument like `--target` — `bin/arc.mjs` does `run(INSTALL, ["--self", ...rest.slice(1)])` so `--target opencode` is passed to `arc-install.mjs`, which correctly refuses. But `arc compile --self --source C:\foo` passes through. That's fine. The real gap: `arc compile --self` in a directory that is not the arc checkout (e.g. a consumer project) runs `selfRender` on the *default* tree `resolve(join(HERE, "..", "..", ".."))` which is arc's own source, not the cwd. So a consumer running `arc compile --self` rewrites arc's committed outputs, not the consumer's tree — surprising but not a write outside arc. More dangerous: `--source` is accepted and can point anywhere, so `arc compile --self --source /etc` attempts an lstat walk of `/etc` and reports every file under `/etc/.codex` etc. as extra, but the writer could write into `/etc/.opencode` if the user has permission.
findings.why: `--self` with `--source` allows arbitrary write target with no confinement; any directory can be the render root, so `--source ~` or `--source /` can write `.opencode/` and `.agents/skills/` into directories the user can write, outside any project. Not arc's own guard, but ADR-2023's boundary.
findings.fix: For `--self` (non-check), confine `--source` to an arc checkout: refuse unless `dir` contains `engine/harnesses.yaml` and `AGENTS.md`, or require an explicit `--source` only with `--check`.

findings.breaking_input: The `init into arc itself` test loops targets and asserts `plan:` and `refused [inside-source]` and non-zero exit. But it never asserts the installer did not write anything. If the guard were removed (or only refused after writing), the test would still pass as long as the refusal fires after the plan line. The test is weaker than the defect it pins.
findings.why: A bug that wrote managed files before the refusal would not be caught; only the refusal message is checked, not the absence of writes. This is the `expected failure first` pattern the plan demands (a mutant that reorders write-before-guard passes).
findings.fix: Assert `git status --porcelain` of `$ARC_ROOT` is unchanged after each refused `init --dry-run`, and also after a non-dry-run refuse (which never happens because `--dry-run` is used, so the write path is never exercised). Add a non-dry-run arm.

findings.breaking_input: The replay fixture pins the exact `got`/`want` lines. If `scanSecrets` were to stop scanning the `payload` field entirely (e.g. a refactor that only scans selected keys), the `landed clean` and both controls would all print `clean` and the test would fail on `control hit`, so that's caught. But if the scanner stopped scanning `process` (where the adjacency bug lived) and the URL cases still clean while the split control still hits through another join, the test passes while the specific bug could recur. Weak but acceptable.
findings.why: The test only proves the four URL cases are clean and two forms of a DSN still hit; it does not pin that the scanner scans the entire canonical envelope (the `process` field specifically). A regression that skips `process` would not be caught unless a control depends on it.
findings.fix: Add a control that only matches via the `process` adjacency (e.g. a URL ending right before `"process":` with an `@` in process), and assert it is clean now and would have hit before.

findings.breaking_input: The reap test uses `sleep 10` then checks the grandchild marker absent. If the fake grandchild takes up to 9000ms and the kill happens at the wrong moment, the 10s sleep may be insufficient (set FAKE_OC_GRANDCHILD_MS=9000, kill earlier, then sleep 10 from end of second wrap — the grandchild could still be alive 9s after the first run was killed, and 10s after the `sleep 10` starts, so marker may appear just after). The test can pass spuriously if the grandchild was already killed (fine) or flakily fail if timing is tight. More importantly, `reapStale` on POSIX kills the leader's group only (L5), so the grandchild — if it survived `killTree` of the first run because it detached — would be reaped by the second run's `reapStale`, which only checks the leader pid's command line (`opencode`), not grandchildren. The grandchild's command line is whatever the fake is; if it names opencode it's killed, else it survives and the sleep check fails — but only if the grandchild actually detached, which the fixture may not set up on POSIX.
findings.why: The test only proves the grandchild is gone after the reap; it does not prove the reap found and killed a detached grandchild on POSIX (the code path doesn't walk the tree there), so the test passes even though L5 leaves POSIX orphans unreaped.
findings.fix: Add a POSIX assertion: spawn a detached grandchild (setsid) via the fake and assert `reapStale` kills it and the second run refuses or reaps it. Currently the POSIX path cannot pass such a test.
